questions.problem:
$$
Find a hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).$
questions.worked_solution:
$$
Osborn's rule allows us to construct a hyperbolic identity from a corresponding trigonometric identity.

To apply Osborn's rule, we follow two steps:

1\. Replace every trigonometric function with its corresponding hyperbolic function.

2\. For any product of two trigonometric sines, flip the sign of the corresponding product of hyperbolic sines.

We're given the following trigonometric identity:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)
$$

Notice that we have a product of sines. Therefore, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡y & =\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x+y)-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(x-y).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x{sech}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identity that corresponds to the trigonometric identity 

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identity is

$$
\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral using the above identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x{sech}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\cdot {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x})}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{1}{{cosh}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\operatorname{tanh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{tanh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}-0 \\  & =\frac{2-{2}^{-1}}{2+{2}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{2-\frac{1}{2}}{2+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{\frac{5}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities corresponding to the trigonometric identities 

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\,\text{ and }\,\operatorname{sech}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral using the above identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sech}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sinh}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cosh}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-\operatorname{sinh}⁡0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{0}-{e}^{-0}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2-{2}^{-1}}{2}-\frac{1-1}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}

$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{coth}⁡x}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{coth}⁡x}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{csch}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}\cdot {sinh}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=\operatorname{cosh}⁡x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\frac{5}{3}$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\operatorname{cosh}⁡x\operatorname{sinh}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{5/3}u\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}{|}_{1}^{5/3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{25}{9}-1) \\  & =\frac{8}{9}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}2\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

First, we find the hyperbolic identities that correspond to the following trigonometric identities:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}
$$

Using Osborn's rule, the corresponding hyperbolic identities are

$$
\operatorname{coth}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡x}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x},\,\operatorname{csch}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we rewrite the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}2\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2x.$ Then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2x.$

| $x$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡16$ |

Now, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\operatorname{csch}⁡(2x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡16}\operatorname{csch}⁡(u)\operatorname{coth}⁡(u)\,\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡(u){|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡16} \\  & =-\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡16)+\operatorname{csch}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡16)}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sinh}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{16-{16}^{-1}}{2})}+\frac{1}{(\frac{4-{4}^{-1}}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(\frac{255}{32})}+\frac{1}{(\frac{15}{8})} \\  & =\frac{104}{255}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
